\section[tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr]{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير} (tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr) — wishing the morning, not the night}

\label{lesson:AR-C27-tusbih-ala-khayr}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Every "good night" you've learned in other languages wishes a peaceful \textbf{night}. Arabic's everyday version does something completely different — it skips the night and wishes the \textbf{morning} instead.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير} — "may you wake into goodness"}
\textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} (\textbf{tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr}) is the most common everyday Arabic "good night" — but it literally means "\textbf{may you wake up into goodness}." Break it down:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{تصبح}} (\emph{tuṣbiḥ}) — the ordinary imperfect ("you become") of \textbf{\ar{أصبح}} (\emph{aṣbaḥa}, "\textbf{to become morning, to wake up}") — the \textbf{exact same root}, \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}} (ṣ-b-ḥ), as \textbf{ṣabāḥ} in \textbf{ṣabāḥ al-khayr} ("good morning," Chapter 1). No special subjunctive or jussive form is involved — a plain statement doing the work of a blessing, the same way English "you'll sleep well" can function as a wish without any special grammar.
  \item \textbf{\ar{على}} (\emph{ʿalā}) — "upon."
  \item \textbf{\ar{خير}} (\emph{khayr}) — "\textbf{goodness}" — the same word already met in \textbf{masāʾ al-khayr} ("good evening").
\end{itemize}

Put together: not "sleep well," but "\textbf{may your waking be good}." (This particular form, \emph{tuṣbiḥ}, addresses one \textbf{man}; a woman is \emph{tuṣbiḥī} {[}\ar{تصبحي}{]}, a group is \emph{tuṣbiḥū} {[}\ar{تصبحوا}{]}.)

\begin{culture}
Here's the genuinely different part: \textbf{every} other "good night" in this arc — English, French, German, Spanish — wishes something about the \textbf{night itself}. Arabic's everyday version does the opposite: it's grammatically about the \textbf{morning that follows}, built from the same "waking" root already hiding in \emph{ṣabāḥ}. Notice what's genuinely absent: \textbf{\ar{ليل}} (\emph{layl}, "night," last lesson) doesn't appear anywhere in this phrase at all. It reuses pieces you already have (\emph{ṣ-b-ḥ}, \emph{khayr}) but points them at a \textbf{different moment in time} than every other language's farewell.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr" — literally "may you wake into goodness"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the shared root — tuṣbiḥ and ṣabāḥ, both from ṣ-b-ḥ{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest twist — this "good night" is really about the morning, not the night{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} literally mean? ("\textbf{May you wake up into goodness}.") What root does \emph{tuṣbiḥ} share with \emph{ṣabāḥ al-khayr}? (\emph{\textbf{Ṣ-b-ḥ}}, "morning/to become morning.") Unlike English, French, and German's "good night," what moment in time does Arabic's everyday version actually point to? (\textbf{The morning that follows}, not the night itself.)
\end{tcolorbox}
